column2: Gilgameš said to him, to Ūta-napišti the Far-away:

I keep looking at you, Ūta-napišti:
3	your measurements are not different — you are as I am;
4	you yourself are not different — you are as I am.
5	My heart was wholly set on doing battle with you,
6	[yet ... ] my arm lies idle against you.
7	[Yo]u — how did you come to stand in the assembly of the gods and hunt out life?
Ūta-napišti said to him, to Gilgameš:

Let me open to you, Gilgameš, a guarded matter;
10	let me tell you a secret of the gods.
11	Šuruppak — a city you yourself know,
12	[a city] set on the bank of the Euphrates —
13	that city was old, and gods were inside it,
14	and the great gods' heart moved them to make the Flood.
15	Their father Anu sw[or]e the oath,
16	their counsellor the fighter Enlil,
17	their throne-bearer Ninurta,
18	their canal-master Ennugi;
19	Ea the Prince was under oath along with them —
20	so he repeated their word to a fence of reeds:
21	'Reed fence, reed fence! Wall, wall!
22	Reed fence, listen! Wall, take note!
23	Man of Šuruppak, son of Ubar-Tutu:
24	tear down the house; build a boat.
25	Abandon wealth; go looking for the living.
26	Despise property; keep breath alive.
27	Take up into the boat the seed of every living thing.
28	The boat you are to build —
29	let her measurements be measured out;
30	let her beam and her length answer one another;
31	roof her over like the Apsû.'
32	I understood, and I said to Ea my lord:
33	'I ob[ey,] my lord, what you have said, just so;
34	I have marked it; I will do it.
35	But h[ow] shall I answer the city — the crowd and the elders?'
36	Ea shaped his mouth to speak,
37	saying to me, his servant:
38	'Then you, say to them this:
39	[Sur]ely Enlil has come to hate me;
I can dwell in [yo]ur city no longer;
[on] Enlil's ground I can set my [fo]ot no more.
[I will go do]wn to the Apsû, to dwell with Ea my lord —
and [on y]ou he will rain down plenty:
[a wealth] of birds, a bounty(?) of fishes,
[ ... ] riches and harvest;
in the morning, bread-cakes(?);
in the evening he will rain down on you a shower of wheat."'
At the first of the morning's brightening,
at the gate of Atra-hasīs the lan[d] was gathering:
the carpenter carrying [his] adz[e,]
the reed-worker carrying [his] sto[ne,]
[the shipwright(?) carrying] hi[s] heavy axe;
the young men [ ... ;]
the old men hauling rope of palm-fibre;
the rich man carrying the pitch;
the poor man brought the tackle [ ... ]
On the fifth day I set down her shape:
one field her floor-plan; ten rods tall her sides;
ten rods each way the rim of her deck.
I laid down her hull; I drew her out.
I gave her six decks;
I divided her sevenfold;
her interior I cut into nine.
Water-plugs I drove into her waist;
I saw to the punting-poles and laid in the stores.
Three times thirty-six hundred (measures) of pitch I poured into the kiln;
three times thirty-six hundred of bitumen I put inside;
three times thirty-six hundred (measures the) basket-bearers hauled of oil,
besides the thirty-six hundred of oil the offering consumed
and the twice thirty-six hundred of oil the boatman stowed away.
I slaughtered oxen past counting;
I killed sheep every day;
ale, beer, oil, and wine
[I gave] my crews to drink like river-water,
and they made festival as on the days of the New Year itself.
At the ris[ing] of the sun I set my hand to the oiling;
[be]fore the sun's setting the boat was finished.
[The launching(?)] was a hard torment:
we kept shifting rollers(?) fore and aft
[until] two-thirds of her [we]nt in.
Everything I had I loaded on her:
everything I had of silver I loaded on her;
everything I h[ad] of gold I loaded on her;
everything I ha[d I loa]ded on her — the seed of every living thing.
I brought up in[to] the boat all my family and kin;
the herds of the steppe, the beasts of the steppe, the sons of every craft I brought aboard.
Šamaš had set me the appointed hour:
'In the morning, bread-cakes(?); in the evening he will rain down a shower of wheat —
then enter the boat and seal your hatch.'
That hour arrived:
in the morning, bread-cakes(?); in the evening he rained down a shower of wheat.
I watched the face of the weather:
the weather was terror to behold.
I entered the boat and sealed my hatch;
to the sealer of the boat, to Puzur-Enlil the shipwright,
I handed over the palace with its goods.
At the first of the morning's brightening
there rose up off the base of the sky a black cloud;
inside it Adad was thundering on and on;
Šullat and Haniš were going before it,
the throne-bearers going over mountain and land;
Errakal was wren[ching] out the mooring-poles;
Ninurta, going by, made the weirs overflow;
the Anunnaki lifted torches high,
setting the land ablaze with their glare.
The dead-stillness of Adad crossed the sky,
turning all that was bright to bla[ck]ness.
[He charg]ed the land like an ox [ ... ;] he smash[ed it] like a pot.
For one day the gal[e — the Flood — ... ]
Fast it blew, and [ ... ] the F[lood ... ] the mountain,
passing over the people like battle, [like the weapon of annihilation.]
No brother can see his brother;
no people can be told apart in the destr[uction.]
Even the gods took fright at the Flood:
they drew back; they went up to the heaven of Anu;
the gods, curled up like dogs, lay out in the open.
Ištar was screaming like a woman in labor;
the Lady-of-the-Gods, the sweet-voiced, was wailing:
'Would that that day had turned back to clay —
because I spoke evil in the assembly of the gods!
How could I speak evil in the assembly of the gods,
declare battle for the destruction of my people?
It is I who give birth — these people are mine! —
and now, like the spawn of fishes, they fill the sea!'
The gods of the Anunnaki were weeping with her;
the gods, wrung out, sat wee[ping with her,]
their lips scabbed over, seized with fever-heat.
Six days and seven nights
the wind ran on — downpour, gale — the Flood flattened the land.
On the arrival of the seventh day
the gale slackened; [the Flood ... ;]
the sea, that had thrashed like a woman in labor, grew calm;
the evil wind fell dead-still; the Flood held back.
I looked at the day: silence was laid down,
and all mankind had gone back to clay.
The floodplain lay level like a roof.
I opened a hatch, and daylight fell on the side of my nose.
I crouched down; I sat; I wept;
over the side of my nose my tears kept running.
I searched the coastlines at the rim of the sea:
at fourteen places a region stood up out of the water.
On Mount Nimuš the boat came to rest.
Mount Nimuš held the boat and would not give her up to moving —
one day, a second day, Mount Nimuš held the boat and would not give her up;
a third day, a fourth day, Mount Nimuš held the boat and would not give her up;
a fifth day, a sixth day, Mount Nimuš held the boat and would not give her up.
On the arrival of the seventh day
I brought out a dove and let it go.
The dove went off, and it came back to me:
no standing-place showed for it, so it turned around.
I brought out a swallow and let it go.
The swallow went off, and it came back to me:
no standing-place showed for it, so it turned around.
I brought out a raven and let it go.
The raven went off and saw the ebbing of the water:
it eats, it wades, it bobs its tail — it did not turn around.
I brought (everything) out and offered sacrifice to the four winds;
I strewed incense on the peak of the mountain;
seven and seven cult-vessels I set in place,
and into their bowls I heaped reed, cedar, and myrtle.
The gods smelled the savor;
the gods smelled the sweet savor;
the gods gathered like flies over the man of the sacrifice.
At once, the moment the Lady-of-the-Gods arrived,
she lifted up the great flies Anu had made for his courting:
'You gods — as surely as this lapis is on my neck,
I shall remember these days and never, ever forget.
Let the gods come to the incense —
but let Enlil not come to the incense,
because without taking counsel he made the Flood
and consigned my people to destruction!'
At once, the moment Enlil arrived,
he saw the boat — and Enlil was seized with fury,
filled with rage at the gods, the Igīgī:
'From where did a living thing escape?
No one was to survive the destruction!'
Ninurta shaped his mouth to speak,
saying to the fighter Enlil:
'Who but Ea contrives such a thing?
Ea alone knows every craft.'
Ea shaped his mouth to speak,
saying to the fighter Enlil:
'You, sage of the gods, fighter —
how, how could you make the Flood without taking counsel?
On the bearer of the sin, lay his sin;
on the bearer of the fault, lay his fault.
Slacken the rope, that it not be cut; haul it in, that it not go slack.
Instead of your making the Flood,
a lion could have risen and thinn[ed] the people;
instead of your making the Flood,
a wolf could have risen and thin[ned] the people;
instead of your making the Flood,
famine could have settled and slaugh[tered] the land;
instead of your making the Flood,
Erra could have risen and slaughtered the land.
As for me — I did not open the secret of the great gods:
I let Atra-hasīs see a dream, and he heard the secret of the gods.
And now — take counsel about him.'
Enlil came up into the boat.
He took my hands and brought me up;
he brought up my wife, knelt her at my side;
he touched our brows, and standing between us he blessed us:
'Before now, Ūta-napišti was human.
Now let Ūta-napišti and his wife become like us gods;
let Ūta-napišti live far away, at the mouth of the rivers.'
They took me; far away, at the mouth of the rivers, they settled me.
But as for you — who will gather the gods for you,
so that you find the life you are hunting?
Come, try: do not sleep for six days and seven nights!"
The moment he sat back on his haunches,
sleep like fog was already breathing over him.
Ūta-napišti said to her, to his wife:

Look at the young man who demanded life:
214	sleep like fog is breathing over him.
His wife said to him, to Ūta-napišti the Far-away:
Ūta-napišti said to her, to his wife:

Man is a cheat; he will try to cheat you.
221	Come, bake his daily loaves; keep setting them by his head,
222	and mark on the wall the days that he sleeps.
So she baked his daily loaves; she kept setting them by his head,
and noted on the wall the days that he slept.
His first loaf is dried out;
the second is leathery; the third is soggy;
the fourth crust has gone white;
the fifth has thrown its bloom of mould;
the sixth is fresh-baked;
the seventh — still on the coals — and he touched him, and the man awoke.
Gilgameš said to him, to Ūta-napišti the Far-away:

The instant sleep spilled over me,
233	that instant you touched me and roused me!
Ūta-napišti [said] t[o him,] to Gilgameš:
Gilgameš said to him, to Ūta-napišti the Far-away:

[Wha]t shall I do, Ūta-napišti? Where shall I go?
244	The Thief has taken hold of my [flesh:]
245	in my own bedroom death is sitting,
246	and wherever [I turn my face] — there too is death!
Ūta-napišti said to [him,] to Ur-šanabi the boatman:
Ur-šanabi took him and brought him to the washtub;
he washed his matted hair clean as snow(?) in water;
he threw off his pelts, and the sea carried them away;
his body was rinsed to fairness;
the ker[chief of] his head was made new;
he was clothed in a robe, the garment of his dignity.
Until he should go [home to his city,]
until he should arrive at the end of his road,
[the robe would show no st]ain, but stay new and yet new.
Gilgameš and Ur-šanabi boarded the boat;
they launched the c[raf]t, and the two of them rode it.
His wife said to him, to Ūta-napišti the Far-away:

Gilgameš came here; he toiled; he strained.
275	What have you given him to carry home to his land?
And at that, he — Gilgameš — lifted the pole
and brought the boat back in to the shore.
Ūta-napišti [said t]o him, to Gilgameš:

Gilgameš, you came here; you toiled; you strained.
280	What shall I give you to carry home to your land?
281	Let me open, Gilgameš, a guarded matter;
282	let me te[ll you] a secret [of the gods.]
283	There is a plant — its [form] is [f]ashioned like boxthorn;
284	its spine, like the briar's, will pri[ck your hands.]
285	If your hands can reach that plant, [you will find life(?).]
Gilgameš, on hearing this,
opened a ch[annel ... ;]
he bound heavy stones [on his feet;]
they dragged him down to the Aps[û ... ;]
he took the plant and wren[ched it up ... ;]
he cut loose the heavy stones [from his feet,]
and the sea threw him up onto its shore.
Gilgameš said to him, to Ur-šanabi the boatman:

Ur-šanabi — this plant is the plant of heartbeat:
296	by it a man can reach again the breath of his life.
297	I will carry it home to Uruk-the-Sheepfold;
298	I will feed it to an old man, and so put the plant to the test.
299	Its name shall be 'Old-Man-Grown-Young.'
300	Then I will eat it myself, and go back to how I was in my youth.
At twenty leagues they broke off a morsel;
at thirty leagues they set up the night's camp.
Gilgameš saw a pool whose water was cold;
he went down into it and was bathing in the water.
A snake caught the scent of the plant;
[in sil]ence it came up and carried the plant away;
turning back, it dropped its slough.
Then and there Gilgameš sat down weeping;
over the side of his nose his tears kept running.
[ ... , say]ing to Ur-šanabi the boatman:

[For] whose sake, Ur-šanabi, did my arms grow tired?
312	For whose sake did the blood of my heart run dry?
313	I got no good thing for myself;
314	I did the good deed for the lion of the ground.
315	Already the tide is lifting twenty leagues off,
316	and when I opened the channel I threw down my tackle there —
317	what landmark could I find that was set for me? I should have drawn back sooner —
318	and the boat I left on the shore!
At twenty leagues they broke off a morsel;
at thirty leagues they set up the night's camp.
They arrived inside Uruk-the-Sheepfold.
Gilgameš said to him, to Ur-šanabi the boatman:

Go up, Ur-šanabi, on the wall of Uruk; walk its circuit.
324	Test the platform; consider the brickwork:
325	is its brick not brick fired in a kiln?
326	Did the Seven Counsellors not lay down its footing?
327	A šār of city, a šār of orchard, a šār of clay-pit, the open ground of Ištar's house:
328	three šār and the open ground — the survey of Uruk.
